title: Randomify
meta: Draws one random song from a corpus built out of MusicBrainz and links it on eight streaming services.
body: One spin. The card shows the drawn recording, its cover art, a 30-second preview, and a button for each service that has it. Randomify is a shuffle button pointed at everything ever recorded. Each press draws one song from a corpus built out of MusicBrainz , plays a 30-second preview, and shows buttons that open the same track on Spotify, Apple Music, YouTube Music, Tidal, Deezer, Amazon Music, and, when an exact link exists, Pandora and Bandcamp. The interesting problems were what "random" should mean over a catalog where popularity follows a long tail , drawing a song in one database round trip, and turning a MusicBrainz recording into working links on services that mostly don't want to be linked to. Tempered sampling Uniform sampling over songs would let an artist with 2,000 registered recordings come up a thousand times more often than one with two singles, and crowded genres would drown out everything else. Uniform over artists overcorrects the other way. So a spin walks down a hierarchy: a facet value, then an artist, then a release group, then a recording, where the facet is one of genre, decade, country, or language, picked at random per spin. At every level a node with \(n\) streamable songs beneath it is chosen with probability \[ P(i) = \frac{n_i^{\alpha}}{\sum_j n_j^{\alpha}}, \qquad \alpha = 0.4. \] At \(\alpha = 0\) every branch is equally likely and obscure artists are heavily over-weighted. I picked 0.4 by ear and the app has no knob for it. One query per spin The tempered weights are precomputed into prefix-sum tables, indexed on partition and cumulative weight, for each facet value, each artist within a facet value, and each release group within an artist. Picking a node is a point lookup: scale a uniform draw by the partition total and take the first row whose cumulative weight crosses it. The Worker generates the draws, and one SQL query of chained CTEs resolves all four levels, joins the display metadata, and aggregates the platform links as JSON. Finding the song The corpus is anchored on Deezer because its API looks up by ISRC without authentication. The resolver spaces requests 220 ms apart, about 4.5 a second, under Deezer's limit of 50 per 5 seconds, and a recording enters the corpus only if the lookup returns an exact match with a playable preview. I don't trust the match blindly. Candidate and query are normalized (diacritics stripped, featuring credits and remaster tags removed) and scored with a Sorensen-Dice coefficient over token sets, title weighted 0.5, artist 0.3, duration agreement 0.2. Even an ISRC hit needs 0.5, because a wrong ISRC in MusicBrainz or on the platform would otherwise ship a wrong link. Deezer preview URLs expire within hours, so I store a stable /preview/{id} path and the Worker mints a fresh URL at play time, answering with a 302 cached at the edge for 45 seconds. randomify.net Source

title: JamStream
meta: A desktop app for playing music together over the internet, on a server that rents itself for the evening and then deletes itself.
body: Eight musicians in a session, each with a fader in my monitor mix, and the latency readout in the corner at 28.0 ms mouth to ear. Sound travels about a foot per millisecond. Two musicians ten feet apart on a stage are already playing ten milliseconds in each other's past, and an orchestra spans several times that. Somewhere around 30 ms the delay stops being room acoustics and starts being lag, and by 70 ms you're not playing together anymore, you're taking turns. A video call runs 150 to 300 ms mouth to ear and nobody minds, since conversation can take turns and music can't. JamStream is a desktop app for jamming over the internet at latencies you can play on. One musician hosts. The app launches a session server on their own computer or in their own cloud account, mints one invite link per seat, and everyone else pastes theirs. Up to ten musicians play, up to twenty listeners tune in, the session can stream to Twitch and YouTube and record takes into the host's own bucket, and when the music stops the server deletes itself. Where 30 ms goes I set the target at under 30 ms mouth to ear. The network is paid twice, your uplink and everyone's downlink. Measured medians with real Opus and real encryption over a simulated network are 14.7 ms at a 1 ms round trip to the server, 24.3 ms at a same-region 12 ms round trip, and 69.8 ms coast to coast over 45 ms of DSL. The session server runs a mix tick every 2.5 ms, which is 120 samples at 48 kHz. Each tick it decodes every musician's uplink, builds one personal stereo mix per musician with that musician left out, applies that member's fader and constant-power pan, and encodes the result back at 192 kbps. You're left out of your own mix because you monitor yourself locally through your hardware, and at low latency a mix that includes your own signal late is unplayable. The jitter buffer's blind spot The jitter buffer is mostly textbook. There's a failure mode between the ordinary recovery paths. If a packet arrives one frame behind the playout position and that pull was concealed, playout steps back a frame. If arrivals jump 512 frames, that reads as a stream restart and the buffer resets. Between those two lies a hole. A persistent offset of 2 to 511 frames means every packet is slightly late, every pull conceals, and both escape hatches are out of reach forever. The signature is a concealed pull with nothing playable on a tick that also dropped a late packet, and if it persists for 60 ticks the buffer abandons its playout position and re-anchors. Renting a server for the evening A rented server that outlives the jam is a subscription you didn't sign up for, so teardown is a dead man's switch that lives in the guest, never on your laptop. While musicians are connected, the server touches an activity file once a second. A systemd timer compares that file's age against the idle window (default 10 minutes) and the session's hard cap (default 12 hours). The guard measures both in /proc/uptime seconds and never subtracts wall-clock timestamps, because a cloud VM routinely boots with a wrong hardware clock and takes a large NTP step a minute later. A wall-clock idle window would read that step as ten minutes of silence and destroy a server with musicians playing on it. Three hours of a four-piece costs about $0.08. Downloads and Guide Source

title: Sprouts
meta: Conway and Paterson's pen-and-paper game in the browser, against an AI that solves the board with nimbers where it can and draws its lines through a triangulation of the face.
body: Ten moves into a game on nine spots. The move list says what each line did. Sprouts is a pen-and-paper game that John Conway and Michael Paterson invented at Cambridge in 1967. You start with \(n\) dots, called spots. A move draws a curve from one spot to another, or from a spot back to itself, without crossing any existing line, and then puts a new spot somewhere on that curve. No spot may have more than three lines touching it. Whoever makes the last legal move wins. I wanted to play it against a computer. The position without the drawing The first version of this treated the board as a picture. It rasterized the lines, thinned the free space to a skeleton, and pathfound along that, and legality was a pixel test. It was slow and wrong in both directions. At one point it declared a game over with a legal move still on the board. The rewrite keeps the drawing out of the rules. A position is a rotation system : each spot lists its lines in counterclockwise order, and that alone determines the faces, which is everything Sprouts cares about. The search Sprouts is an impartial game, so every position has a nimber, and a position made of independent parts has the XOR of its parts' nimbers. The player to move loses exactly when that sum is zero. A move changes one face, but a spot with two lines has a corner in each face beside it, so faces that share a live spot are one game. The faces linked that way are the regions, and each is solved on its own. Who wins is a different question. Applegate, Jacobson, and Sleator computed it by exhaustive search up to 11 spots in 1991 and conjectured that the first player wins exactly when \(n \bmod 6\) is 3, 4, or 5. Lemoine and Viennot carried the pattern to 44 spots by computing nimbers , one value for each independent part of the board instead of one search over the whole thing. Nobody has proved it in general. The AI here does the same thing on smaller boards. When every region is small enough to solve within a budget, about a quarter of a second, the AI plays a move that leaves a zero sum, or when there isn't one, the move that leaves the opponent the most room. Six fresh spots have 18 lives between them and are already too much to solve from cold, so bigger positions go to an alpha-beta search with iterative deepening under an 800 ms clock. Drawing the move The search picks a move in the model, and then it has to be drawn. Lines keep a clearance from other lines and from spots so the board stays readable and later moves have somewhere to go. The router erodes the face by those clearances, pushing every wall inward and cutting a disc around every spot except the move's two ends, and triangulates what's left with a constrained Delaunay triangulation . Any path through the free triangles keeps the clearances by construction, and if the two ends are in different pieces of the eroded face, there is no room. Everything in this pipeline is sums, products, and square roots, no trig and no hypot, because the WebAssembly build has to draw the same curve bit for bit as the native one or a shared game comes out different on the other end. Live Demo Source

title: ooooh
meta: An iPhone app for thinking out loud with a patient listener.
body: I think better out loud, but the usual note-taking apps are just speaking into the void, with no feedback. So it's difficult to form a coherent note sometimes. Chatbots fill that gap partially, but speak too frequently. That's why I built ooooh . Asking at the right time Early versions would interrupt me. I tried having the voice pause when I started to speak, but on speakerphone it would catch some of its own audio as me talking and stop itself. The balance was to have it speak less often, be really sure I've finished talking, and then confidently say something without listening to itself. A lot of the time went into calibrating Jev so the questions come at the right moment. I recorded about ten sessions and used my experience with them to guide the tuning. Using it I use it to take voice notes. A small but mighty group of beta testers gives me feedback before I launch, mostly on the quality of the questions. ooooh.app Source

title: Squares
meta: A photo redrawn as a squared rectangle, where Kirchhoff's laws pick every square size and a search over planar networks picks the arrangement.
body: A squared rectangle is a rectangle tiled by squares. I wanted to drop a photo on a page and get it back as one of these, with each square colored by the picture underneath. Try it Source

title: String

body: Turns a photo into a few thousand chords between pins on a circle, then prints the build guide. Play Source

title: Deconflict
meta: Assigns WiFi channels by coloring an interference graph built from a floorplan.
body: Two WiFi access points on the same channel with overlapping coverage contend for airtime, and both lose throughput. Picking channels so that no two overlapping APs share one is vertex coloring on an interference graph. Try it Source

title: Sequence Atlas
meta: A map of the OEIS. Every integer sequence is a point, placed beside the sequences that behave like it.
body: The OEIS has about 390,000 integer sequences and the only way to move between them is by cross reference or by searching for terms. I wanted to see the whole thing at once. Try it Source

title: miditool
meta: Sits between my keyboard and the DAW and rewrites what I play, with 52 seeded effects and a hot-reloading KDL config.
body: miditool is a Rust command-line program that sits between a MIDI keyboard and a DAW. I built it to play live on an 88-key piano, and that fixed the constraints before I wrote any effects. Try it Source

title: Time
meta: Two clocks, one on Earth and one on a ship you fly around the Sun, a neutron star, or Sagittarius A*, with the drift between them computed from real geodesics.
body: One clock on the page sits at sea level on Earth and shows your actual local time. The other left Earth in sync with it when the page loaded and is now on a ship around whichever body you picked. play time.seanre.id source github.com/sean-reid/time

title: How Will I Die
meta: What people of your age, sex, and country eventually die of, projected forward from WHO mortality data.
body: Pick a country, an age, and a sex, and I give you a ranked list of what people like you eventually die of, with a rough likelihood next to each. The numbers describe a population rather than you. Try it Source

title: Kakeya
meta: The Kakeya needle problem told in pictures that are computations: Perron trees, Pál joins, and a needle that never leaves the set it sweeps.
body: In 1917 Soichi Kakeya asked how little area you need to turn a unit needle all the way around in the plane, so that it ends up pointing the opposite way. In 1928 Besicovitch showed there's no least area at all. Cut a triangle into slivers, slide them into each other, and the needle can still turn through every direction the triangle covered, in as little room as you like. Play Source

title: OEIS Pi Search
meta: Where the first terms of any OEIS sequence first appear in a billion digits of pi, answered from a Worker with byte-range reads and no database for the digits.
body: Type an OEIS A-number, a sequence name, a few terms, or a string of digits, and the site tells you how far into pi you have to go before the first \(k\) terms appear. The search covers the first 1,000,000,000 digits and strings up to 12 digits long. play oeis-pi-search.seanre.id source github.com/sean-reid/oeis-pi-search

title: Pulse
meta: Heart rate, breathing rate, and HRV estimated from a webcam in the browser, with the pulse painted back onto the face.
body: Each heartbeat pushes blood into the capillaries of the face and shifts the skin color by a fraction of a pixel value. A webcam records that shift even though nobody can see it. Remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) is the name for pulling a pulse waveform back out of it. This one runs entirely in the browser from a laptop camera. Try it Source

title: Clowns and Mimes
meta: Team tag in the dark on a torus or Klein bottle, online or against bots.
body: I made this for fun and community. I wanted to start a Discord server and hang out with friends now and then, so I built a game we could play together: team tag in the dark, on a torus or a Klein bottle . It's an online multiplayer game, but it can be played offline too, against bots. That meant duplicating the bot logic in the Godot client and the TypeScript server, so a code generation step keeps the constants in sync between them. The source has both.

title: Movie Quotes
meta: A film quote quiz: pick which of three lines is from the movie.
body: Just a fun game I made because I know a bunch of film quotes and wanted to challenge myself. Play it or read the source .

title: Rhythm
meta: Drum patterns from Markov chains stacked on Markov chains, with the whole piece carried in its URL.
body: Rhythm plays drum patterns that come out of a stack of Markov chains. The bottom of the stack is a pool of short patterns I call atoms. play rhythm.seanre.id source github.com/sean-reid/rhythm

title: Cyclical
meta: An exhaustive search for chord progressions that loop back to their first chord, streamed from Rust in a Web Worker.
body: Cyclical searches for chord progressions that close their own loop. The solver is Rust compiled to WebAssembly, running in a Web Worker, and it enumerates every cycle that fits. Try it Source

title: Eigencircuits
meta: A fake arXiv for mathematics. A seeded grammar writes the papers and pdfTeX compiles them in the browser.
body: Eigencircuits is an arXiv that publishes only nonsense. Between 30 and 50 new papers appear every day. Play Source

title: Discern
meta: A game that tests how well you tell real photos from generated ones.
body: A game to test your ability to tell real from AI images. In a world of prevalent deepfakes, this ability is becoming really important. Play Source

title: Rebase
meta: A daily puzzle where you assign number bases, some of them irrational, to four digit strings.
body: You assign one base to each string, every base used once, and the four values have to add up to a target. The string 1110 is worth 1110 in base 10, 39 in base 3, 14 in base 2, and about 8.472 in base \(\varphi\). Play Source

title: Polish Notation
meta: A converter between Łukasiewicz's parenthesis-free notation and conventional logic notation, with LaTeX output.
body: Polish notation puts every logical operator before its arguments. The conventional \((p \land q) \to r\) becomes CKpqr: C for implication, K for conjunction, then the three variables in order. I built a page that takes a formula in either notation, works out which one it is, and renders both, with the LaTeX a click away. Try it Source

title: Lipreadle
meta: A daily Wordle-style puzzle where you read the word off someone's lips.
body: A spin on Wordle: guess the word being said by reading someone's lips. It got surprisingly popular in my friend group and has a small following. play lipreadle.seanre.id source github.com/sean-reid/lipreadle

title: Wason
meta: A procedurally generated daily Wason selection task.
body: I found the Wason puzzles fascinating, so I made a procedurally generated challenge based on them so others could explore them better. Source .

title: Gravity Well Arena
meta: A space shooter where you fly real orbits toward a black hole.
body: I've always wanted to make a game where you control your orbit like a real spaceship would. Black holes are also really interesting subjects for a game. They play into the storyline: as you get closer and closer to the event horizon, aliens appear and make your life difficult. Play Source

title: Severed
meta: Cut submarine cables on a map of 930 metros and 1,644 links and see which cities lose bandwidth.
body: The usual figure is that around 95 percent of intercontinental traffic goes over submarine cables. When several fail in the same chokepoint, countries drop off. Try it Source

title: Voting
meta: Four voting methods checked against Arrow's criteria by enumerating every three-voter profile.
body: Arrow's theorem (1951) says that with three or more candidates, no way of turning a set of individual rankings into one group ranking can satisfy four conditions at once. I wrote a scroll-through explainer in seven chapters with a sandbox at the end where you set three voters' rankings over three candidates, pick a method, and watch the checker find a counterexample. play seanre.id/voting source github.com/sean-reid/voting

title: Antipodal
meta: A globe that shows the weather at any point and at its antipode, over 85 years of ERA5 reanalysis.
body: The Borsuk-Ulam theorem, proved by Karol Borsuk in 1933, says that any continuous map from the sphere to the plane sends some pair of antipodal points to the same value. Take temperature and sea-level pressure as the two coordinates and the theorem says that at every instant, somewhere on Earth, two diametrically opposite points have the same temperature and the same pressure. Antipodal looks at how close real weather data gets to that. Try it Source

title: Tron
meta: Lightcycles in the browser against AI opponents.
body: One of my first programming experiences was making Snake on a TI-84 calculator. This project hearkens back to then, with the added twist of AI lightcycle opponents. Play Source

title: Lacuna
meta: A two-player game where you draw the board as you play and score the regions you close off.
body: Lacuna starts as an empty circle with 12 anchor points around the rim. Two players take turns drawing strands inside it, and the strands become the board. When a region ends up bounded entirely by one player's strands, it seals and scores for that player. I designed the game and its rules from scratch. You could play it with two pens and a printed circle, but tracking which regions have closed is tedious by hand, and the web version does that for you. Source .

title: LaTeX Preview
meta: A LaTeX editor that compiles to PDF in the browser, with pdfTeX in WebAssembly and a self-hosted TeX Live subset.
body: LaTeX Preview is a two-pane editor that compiles TeX to PDF in the browser. There's no server to send the document to. Try it Source

title: URL Extension Service
meta: A URL lengthener that encodes the destination inside the long link, so it needs no database and nothing expires.
body: URL shorteners die and take their links with them. I built the opposite. You give urls.dwainosaur.com a destination and a length from 100 to 2,000 characters, and it hands back a link that long. Play Source

title: Pikiwedia
meta: A proxy that serves live Wikipedia with its word onsets swapped, the same way on every visit.
body: Pikiwedia is a Cloudflare Worker that proxies English Wikipedia and spoonerizes it. Play Source

title: The Infinite Keynote
meta: A fictional tech keynote that streams forever, where the clock is the only state viewers share.
body: The Infinite Keynote is a product launch that never ends. Everyone watching sees the same speaker saying the same sentence at the same moment, and nothing on the server keeps track of any of it. play keynote.dwainosaur.com source github.com/sean-reid/keynote

title: Sounds
meta: A voxel world where the music is generated from the biome you're standing in.
body: Walk through a generated voxel world and everything you hear is composed on the spot from where you are. In the dunes the scale flips to Phrygian dominant with a flamenco bass line, and deep ocean slows everything to a Lydian drone. play seanre.id/sounds source github.com/sean-reid/sounds

title: Points
meta: Click points on a grid and get the simplest integer-coefficient curve through them.
body: In 5th grade I played a game called Green Globs. Green dots were scattered on a coordinate plane and I had to type an equation whose graph passed through as many as possible. Points does the reverse, where I click a few points on a grid and the computer finds a curve through all of them, as an exact implicit equation with small integer coefficients like x² + y² = 25 or x · y = 6. Try it Source

title: Fourier Phase
meta: Two images pushed to share one Fourier amplitude spectrum, and they still look like themselves.
body: This app takes two images you upload, pushes them toward one shared amplitude spectrum, and shows that they still look like themselves. Try it Source

title: Captcha Royale
meta: A battle royale where every round is a procedurally generated CAPTCHA and a wrong answer knocks you out.
body: Up to 16 players enter a room, a CAPTCHA appears, and a wrong answer or a timeout knocks you out. The puzzles don't have to stop a bot, so I could make them as hard as I liked. Play Source

title: Crossword Generator
meta: Crossword grids as a SAT problem, plus a CLI that turns them into print-ready puzzle books.
body: I noticed crossword puzzle books selling well on Amazon KDP and wanted to see if I could automate the whole thing from one command, grids and clues through page layout, cover, and a print-ready PDF. Try it Source

title: Antibook
meta: Project Gutenberg books with every word I could invert replaced by its antonym.
body: Antibook takes books from the Project Gutenberg catalog and replaces every word it can with an antonym. Sentence structure survives and the meaning flips. play antibook.dwainosaur.com source github.com/sean-reid/antibook

title: Gardener's Dilemma
meta: A two-player harvesting game with the Collatz sequence as its clock.
body: Five vines, each a number. Every 2.5 seconds every vine takes one Collatz step: halve it if even, triple it and add 1 if odd. Harvesting a vine scores its current value. A harvest chains if its value appears within 25 Collatz steps of your last one, and chains multiply the score. The dilemma is whether to grab the tall vine now or wait for one that chains. A vine at 76 will be 38 on the next tick. play gardeners-dilemma.seanre.id source github.com/sean-reid/gardeners-dilemma

title: Mastery
meta: 100 skills scored by hand on 19 difficulty axes, with 12 challenges you can try in the browser.
body: Chess and cardiac surgery might both take a decade, but they differ on failure cost, physical demand, and how fast the field moves under you. So I scored 100 skills on 19 axes, each from 0 to 10 with a cited source, and ranked them. Two skills with the same composite score can have completely different profiles. play seanre.id/mastery source github.com/sean-reid/mastery

title: Bananas for Scale
meta: A static reference site that restates real measurements in bananas, golden retrievers, and other useless units.
body: You look up a thing, get its real measurements, and see them restated in units nobody asked for. The International Space Station orbits at 408 kilometers, or about 2.3 million bananas end to end. Play Source

title: Tongue Simulator
meta: Type a sentence and watch a simulated tongue, jaw, and velum move through it while the browser speaks.
body: Type some text, press Speak, and the browser reads it aloud while drawing a cross-section of the vocal tract, with the tongue, jaw, velum, and lips moving through the articulation for each sound in time with the audio. Play Source

title: Crochet Pattern Generator
meta: Draw one side of a shape and get row-by-row amigurumi stitch counts for it.
body: Draw one side of a shape and get row-by-row amigurumi stitch counts for it. Play Source

title: Meta Tic-Tac-Toe
meta: Ultimate tic-tac-toe against an alpha-beta search written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly.
body: Ultimate tic-tac-toe takes a game that's been solved since childhood and makes it hard. The board is a 3x3 grid of smaller boards, and the cell you play in decides which board your opponent must play in next. The opponent is an alpha-beta search written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly. Play Source

title: Entropy Bus
meta: A racing game where the bus goes faster the less predictable your typing is.
body: The bus accelerates on the Shannon entropy of whatever you type. Hold one key and it crawls. Use everything on the keyboard with no rhythm to it, and it moves. Play Source

title: What ____ Are You?
meta: A personality quiz where the category is a parameter and the answer comes from Wikipedia.
body: Those "What kind of X are you?" quizzes are everywhere. So I built one where the category is a parameter. The result is pulled live from Wikipedia. play what-are-you.dwainosaur.com source github.com/sean-reid/what-are-you

title: Dependencies
meta: Races two ways of finding which declared dependencies a build actually needs.
body: A project declares 100 dependencies and needs a handful. The rest are left over from deleted features or already pulled in by something else. I wanted to see how the two obvious strategies compare, so I made a page that runs both side by side on the same grid of squares. Try it Source

title: FrankenPeanuts
meta: Four random Peanuts panels from 1950 to 2000, stitched into a new strip on every reload.
body: FrankenPeanuts picks four panels at random from the weekday strips and lays them out as a new four-panel comic. Play Source

title: Haiku
meta: A screensaver that generates a new haiku every ten seconds from a small grammar.
body: This page makes a new haiku every ten seconds, fades it in over a slowly moving background, and never stops. The hard constraint is 5, 7, 5 syllables. Try it Source

title: BrainRotter
meta: Fills a page with grammatical brainrot from a weighted grammar and a 2,277-term lexicon.
body: The internet has a dialect, and I wanted to see what happened when I fed its vocabulary into a proper context-free grammar. Press the button and BrainRotter fills the page with paragraphs of grammatically correct brainrot. Play Source

title: NYT Crosswords
meta: An ad-free browser player for New York Times crosswords from 1976 to 2017.
body: The New York Times crossword is behind a paywall, and the official app is full of ads even when you pay. I like doing old crosswords, the ones from the 70s and 80s where the clues reference things that no longer exist. Try it Source

title: Flow
meta: An RSVP speed reader that starts slow and ramps up, so the opening sentence lands.
body: I tried several RSVP apps and they all had the same problem. They start at the target speed. Playback starts at 120 WPM and climbs to the target, 650 by default, over the first 80 words. play seanre.id/flow source github.com/sean-reid/flow featured Featured on Product Hunt

title: Perfect Hindsight
meta: What a dollar becomes if you hold the best S&P 500 stock every single trading day.
body: What if you knew, every morning, which S&P 500 stock would go up the most that day, and put everything in it? One stock per day, long only, no margin. Over 50 years, starting February 13, 1976, a dollar becomes about \(10^{1078}\) dollars. Try it Source

title: Wikipedia Unscrambler
meta: A word game that scrambles a passage from one of yesterday's most-read Wikipedia articles.
body: The typoglycemia meme says you can read jumbled text as long as the first and last letters stay put. That's an overstatement, but context does a lot of the work when you read, and I wanted a game that measured how much. So this scrambles every letter of every word and gives you nothing but the words around it. The passages come from yesterday's most-read Wikipedia articles, so the puzzles rotate on their own. Play Source

title: Anagram Solver
meta: Every way to rearrange a phrase into real words, ranked so the good ones come first.
body: Most anagram sites return one result, maybe two. I wanted all of them for a phrase, with the good ones at the top, and that's a different problem from finding one. Try it Source

title: Lasers
meta: Place and rotate mirrors to bounce a laser around obstacles and into a target.
body: Place and rotate mirrors to bounce the laser around the circles and into the target. Fewer mirrors is a better score. Play Source

title: Papermaker
meta: SCIgen's fake computer science papers, generated in the browser and typeset to PDF.
body: Papermaker is SCIgen in the browser. The papers have the right shape and the right density of jargon and say nothing. play papermaker.dwainosaur.com source github.com/sean-reid/papermaker

title: The Count of Monte Carlo
meta: Random characters settle into the text of Dumas one letter at a time.
body: Each passage starts as noise. Then, on every animation frame, each wrong character gets a 3% chance to snap to its correct value. Play Source

title: Creature Garden
meta: A single-file ecosystem sandbox where procedural creatures eat, breed, and starve on a canvas.
body: Drop some creatures into a space with limited food and see what happens. There's no population equation in the code. Play Source

title: Random Game
meta: Your best next guess in a closest-number-wins game, with the odds drawn on a number line.
body: There's an icebreaker where someone picks a number in a range, say 1 to 100, everyone guesses, and the closest wins. Alone it's binary search. With other people guessing it's a land grab. I built the first version because I was guessing "intuitively" and competing with everyone else's intuition for the same part of the number line. Most people guess round numbers. play seanre.id/random-game source github.com/sean-reid/random-game

title: License Plate Game
meta: Type the three letters from a plate and get the shortest words that contain them in order.
body: There's a road trip game where you take the three letters on a license plate and try to think of a word that contains them in that order, not necessarily adjacent. You see BRN and someone shouts BURNING. I built this to settle arguments. It shows the shortest words first, because in the car a short word is the impressive answer. JAZZ for JZZ wins the round. Play Source
